name: Swiss chard
summary: Colorful leafy greens that keep coming from spring to frost and handle heat better than spinach.
problems: Leaf miners leave pale winding trails in the leaves; pick off spotted leaves and use row cover. Leaf spot shows up in wet weather.
greenhouse_notes: Keeps producing through mild winters in an unheated greenhouse.
notes: Each wrinkled seed is a cluster that sends up several plants; thin to the strongest. Cut outer stalks and leave the center growing.

name: Collard greens
summary: Big, sturdy leaves for slow-cooked greens. Takes both summer heat and frost better than most cabbage relatives.
problems: Cabbage worms, aphids and harlequin bugs; row cover early in the season prevents most of it.
greenhouse_notes: Grows slowly but steadily through winter under cover.
notes: Frost sweetens the leaves. Harvest from the bottom up and one plant can feed you for months. Extra leaves are a treat for goats and chickens.

name: Arugula
summary: Fast, peppery salad leaves ready in about a month. Best in the cool parts of the year.
problems: Flea beetles chew tiny holes in the leaves; row cover helps. Heat makes it bolt and turn bitter fast.
greenhouse_notes: One of the best winter greens for a cold greenhouse.
notes: Sow a short row every two or three weeks. The white flowers are edible and bees like them.

name: Bok choy
summary: Crisp white stems and tender leaves for stir-fries and soups. Quick, and happiest in cool weather.
problems: Bolts to flower in heat or after a cold snap. Flea beetles and slugs like it.
greenhouse_notes: Grows well in a cool greenhouse from fall to spring.
notes: Baby bok choy is ready in about 30 days. Keep the soil evenly moist for tender stems.

name: Turnip
summary: Two crops in one: sweet roots and tender greens, fast in spring and fall.
problems: Root maggots tunnel into roots in cool, wet soil; row cover keeps the flies off. Roots get woody if left too long.
notes: Pull roots when they are 5 to 8 cm (2 to 3 in) across for the sweetest flavor. Roots keep for months in a cool root cellar. Goats enjoy both roots and tops.

name: Leek
summary: A mild, sweet onion relative for soups, grown for its long white stem. Stands in the garden into winter.

preserves.form: Quart bag of frozen sliced leeks

problems: Slow from seed. Onion thrips leave silvery streaks in dry heat.
notes: Hill soil up around the stems as they grow to make more white. Dig them as you need them; most kinds handle frost.

name: Green onion
summary: Bunching onions you cut again and again. Easy from seed and happy in a pot by the kitchen door.
problems: Few problems. Thrips can streak the leaves in hot, dry weather.
greenhouse_notes: Pots of green onions keep growing slowly through winter under cover.
notes: Cut leaves 2.5 cm (1 in) above the base and they grow back. Many bunching kinds come back for years where winters are mild. The root ends of store-bought green onions regrow in a glass of water.

name: Cauliflower
summary: One big head per plant. Fussier than broccoli: it needs steady cool weather, water and food.
problems: Heat, drought or a check in growth makes tiny button heads. Cabbage worms and aphids like it too.
greenhouse_notes: A fall crop finishes well in an unheated greenhouse.
notes: Fall crops are easier than spring ones in hot places. Some kinds need their leaves tied over the head to keep it white.

name: Cantaloupe
summary: Sweet, fragrant melons that love long hot summers. A few vines give you a summer of desserts.

preserves.form: Quart bag of frozen melon cubes

problems: Cucumber beetles and powdery mildew. Too much water near harvest makes melons bland.
greenhouse_notes: Gets an early start in a greenhouse; hand-pollinate flowers if no bees can reach them.
notes: A ripe cantaloupe slips off the vine with a gentle push and smells sweet at the stem end. Support melons on a trellis with slings if you grow them up.

name: Watermelon
summary: The classic summer melon. Needs room, heat and a long season; small "icebox" kinds fit smaller gardens.
problems: Seeds rot in cold soil. Cucumber beetles, aphids and fungal leaf spots in humid weather.
notes: Ripe signs: the curly tendril nearest the melon turns brown, the spot underneath turns from white to creamy yellow, and the rind loses its shine. Goats and chickens enjoy the rinds.

name: Dry beans (pinto and black)
summary: Beans you leave on the plant until the pods are dry and rattle. A pantry staple that keeps for a year or more.
problems: Seeds rot in cold, wet soil. Rain on dry pods can make beans mold; pull whole plants and finish drying them under cover if rain is coming.
notes: Bush kinds are easiest. Plant a block big enough to matter: a 3 m (10 ft) row gives roughly a quart jar of dry beans. They also fix nitrogen and feed the next crop.

name: Tomatillo
summary: Tart green fruits in papery husks, the heart of salsa verde. Grows like a big, sprawling tomato.
problems: One plant alone sets little fruit: grow at least two. Same pests as tomatoes, such as hornworms and flea beetles.
greenhouse_notes: Gets an early start under cover but needs bees to pollinate, so open the doors once it flowers.
notes: Pick when the fruit fills the husk and the husk starts to split. They keep for weeks in the fridge with husks on. Plants reseed freely.
